turns.prompt_text: I've got a problem. I have a bunch of B frames. They are deep frames of the apis meliphera, and these bays have built comb everywhere. Now they're all connected
turns.response_html:
Ah, the dreaded cross-comb and burr comb situation. It is incredibly frustrating when you go to lift a frame and the entire block of wood tries to come up as one giant, sticky, interconnected monolith. Don't worry, every beekeeper deals with this at some point—especially with deep frames where the bees have a lot of vertical real estate to get creative.

When Apis mellifera decides to ignore the foundation and build sideways or bridge everything together, you have to perform a bit of "hive surgery" to get them back on track. If you leave it, inspecting the hive will eventually become impossible without destroying brood and killing bees.

Here is the strategic way to slice, separate, and salvage those deep frames without causing a total colony mutiny.

The Triage Plan

1. Gear Up for Sticky Work

Beyond your usual veil and smoker, you’ll want a few specific tools ready right next to the hive:

  • A long, thin serrated knife (like a bread knife) or a specialized long-bladed capping knife. A standard hive tool is often too thick and blunt to slice cleanly between deep frames.
  • Rubber bands (large size, matching the depth of your frames) or heavy cotton butcher's twine.
  • An empty deep hive body and a catch pan/bucket to hold any wild comb you cut out that can't be saved.

2. Locate the "Starting Thread"

Don't just start hacking into the middle. Look for the outermost frame that is least connected to the hive wall or its neighbor.

  • Blow a little smoke between the top bars to clear the bees so you can see where the structural bridges actually run.
  • Use your knife to slice vertically straight down between the comb faces of frame 1 and frame 2. Keep the knife perfectly parallel to the frames to avoid cutting into the core of the cells.

3. The "Slice and Lift" Technique

Once you've severed the bridge between two frames, use your hive tool to pry the frame straight up, very slowly.

  • If it's cross-combed (built diagonally across multiple frames): You will have to cut the comb away from the frame bars where it shouldn't be.
  • If there is brood in the wild comb: You want to save it. Carefully slice the slab of wild brood comb completely out. Keep it oriented the right way up (sky side up, ground side down).

How to Salvage and Fix the Comb

If you have large sheets of beautiful brood or drawn comb that you had to cut away, you can mount them back into empty frames using the rubber band trick.

Preventing a Repeat Performance

Once you've cleaned up the mess, you have to fix the root cause, or they will do it right again next week. Bees build cross-comb for three main reasons:

  1. Incorrect Frame Spacing: This is the number one culprit. Deep frames must be pushed tightly together in the center of the box. The self-spacing sidebars of Langstroth frames must touch shoulder-to-shoulder. If there are gaps between the top bars, the bees will think it's an invitation to build a bridge.
  2. The Hive Isn't Level: If the hive is leaning significantly to the left or right, the bees will still build their comb perfectly perpendicular to gravity. This means they will start on one top bar and slowly angle right into the neighbor frame as they go down. Check your stand with a bubble level.
  3. Using Foundationless Frames Improperly: If you aren't using wax or plastic foundation, you must checkerboard empty frames between perfectly drawn, straight frames so the bees have a "guide track" to follow.

Take it one slow slice at a time, smoke them gently to keep them calm during the heavy disruptions, and keep a bucket handy for the excess honey and wax!
